cases.title: Python is missing on this PC
cases.story: A session found no usable python on this PC and wrote the fix down. Ten minutes after a compaction dropped the 'no Python' line, a top model typed a python heredoc again.
cases.entry: Python or python3 exits 49 (Microsoft Store stub). A real Python 3.12.14 sits in the Codex app folder. Call that full path, or use node or PowerShell for small JSON work. Check: the path with --version prints 3.12.14.

steps.note: The window points toward Python, because CLAUDE.md names Python 3.12. A summary that said 'no Python' was replaced by one without it.
The owner's design names no trigger. A shell tool error is not a trigger in the earlier knowledge-store design. Only the exit-49 result could start a lookup, after the call.
The error text is word for word and easy to recognise.
One entry matches exactly.
This is the main session. The entry is held until the next compaction, and this session already lost the fact once at a compaction.
Swap python for the full path. A plain JSON script runs on 3.12.
The rerun's exit code decides, at no cost.
The failing model is already the top rung. A stronger model would make the same call.
Python was a side stumble. The earlier knowledge-store design needs a fix commit and a control pair, which a PC fact lacks. Memory got it 29 days later.
The interpreter belongs to another app, which rewrote its folder on 2026-10-21. Newer Pythons arrived later. No repository event marks any of this.

cases.title: Python error, but this project uses uv
cases.story: A subagent typed bare python while its window held the project's 'uv run --locked python' route. It failed, then recovered with diff and grep on the next call.
cases.entry: Same as the python entry, or the memory line. Python is not on PATH in Git Bash (a Windows Store alias); use node for JSON.

steps.note: The project's right route, uv run, was already in the window. The agent typed bare python anyway.
Same as before. No trigger fires before the call.
The error text is the same word for word.
Same error, different right answer. The entry says node or Codex 3.12. This project uses uv with locked 3.13 packages.
The subagent window holds it for its short life.
Fine for a JSON compare. For anything that imports project code it points to the wrong interpreter and away from uv run.
The result is immediate.
The agent is already Opus.
No rule says whether the clinic variant is stored as a sibling, a revision, or not at all.
Two project memories disagree about one PC. EMS says use node for JSON. The clinic says uv run python. The design has no project field.

cases.title: A stored 'no' about tools that exist
cases.story: A design note said no Python and no gh. Six minutes later gh was installed. Python had been in use since 10-06. Clinic memory later stored 'no uv', then uv was installed.
cases.entry: No Python and no gh on this PC. Design around them. Run backend gates only in Docker.

steps.note: A session planning work here would look up which tools exist.
No error occurs when an agent avoids a tool it wrongly believes is missing.
'Is there Python?' is a plain-language question. Only plain-language handles could match it.
The entry is returned. That is the problem.
Any window can hold it.
The cheap model designs around tools that exist, such as Docker-only gates. Nothing it does fails.
A stored 'no' never fails loudly. The agent just does not try. Only a separate review caught it on 11-01.
There is no failure to hand up.
The writer checked PATH only. It wrote 'no gh' six minutes before installing gh, and 'no Python' while Python had been in use since 10-06.
gh arrived 10-31 and uv 11-02. Corrections landed separately in a doc, a memory note and the design. The clinic copy is stale.

cases.title: Bash cuts long heredoc commands
cases.story: Bash commands over about 8 KB fail with an unexpected-EOF error and write nothing. Four later moments repeated it, once by the note's own writer a day after writing it.
cases.entry: A Bash cat heredoc fails at about 9,800 characters with 'unexpected EOF while looking for matching quote'. The file is not written. The tool cuts long commands. Write the file with the Write tool. Dead end: re-sending the heredoc.

steps.note: The entry is in the window, pushed at start. So is the Bash tool's own advice to use a heredoc. They pull opposite ways.
The cost is the failed call itself, 8.6k to 18.6k characters sent twice. A lookup can only follow the error. Nothing fires before the call.
'unexpected EOF while looking for matching' is word for word.
One entry matches exactly.
It was delivered by push into main and subagent windows. The pull-only route in the earlier knowledge-store design would deliver less.
The condition is the length of the agent's next output, which it does not measure.
Exit code 2 comes at once.
Sonnet, Opus and Fable all fail the same way.
First failure was 10-31. The note came on 11-11 after the 40-error peak day, in a batch memory edit, not at a solve.
The limit belongs to the tool version, not a repository. No footprint item sees a tool upgrade.

cases.title: Four agents, same long command, same day
cases.story: Four Opus agents each wrote four slide files in one cat command of 10 to 11k characters. All failed within six seconds. One recovered with four Reads and four Writes.
cases.entry: The Bash heredoc entry from the previous case. That project's memory has no Bash note.

steps.note: This is a different project's memory. It has nothing about Bash limits.
As before, the cost comes before any trigger.
The error text is word for word.
It hits only if the library is shared across projects. The owner says it is. The earlier knowledge-store design is silent.
Four windows opened six seconds apart. No sibling could finish, record and serve another in time.
Nothing was delivered.
The result is immediate.
All agents were Opus.
Four equal solvers of one stumble. The design does not say who writes, or how four near-duplicates merge.
No entry was written.

cases.title: Read cannot open PDF pages here
cases.story: Read on a PDF failed because pdftoppm is missing. The parent found a PowerShell route. Five hours later four new Opus agents hit the same error, because the briefs never mentioned PDFs.
cases.source: Session e56a900a, parent and wave-2 agents
cases.entry: Read with pages on a PDF fails: pdftoppm is not installed. Python is the Store stub. Route: PowerShell reads the bytes, inflates FlateDecode streams and pulls the text. Works for the 41-page Google Docs PDF. Avoid the reserved variable $PID.

steps.note: The brief, written by a parent that knew, has no word 'pdf'. Wave 1 hit the error four seconds before the parent did.
A Read tool error is not on the list of triggers.
The error text is word for word.
This works if the parent's route was stored by 14:16Z.
The subagent window holds it.
Some agents found cheaper pre-extracted text. The entry may pull toward the costlier route.
Text appears or it does not.
Parent and children were all Opus and all failed alike.
It was solved as an aside, with no mid-session capture point. Wave 2 started 5.5 hours later with nothing written. No note ever recorded pdftoppm.
The route depends on how the PDF was made. Pre-extracted text exists for some files in one project only.

cases.title: PDF route, in another project, a month on
cases.story: Research subagents read saved PDFs. The brief named the Codex Python. A Sonnet agent extracted the text in two calls using pypdf. An Opus agent gave up on the PDF.
cases.entry: The PDF entry from the previous case: PowerShell inflate, or the clinic's pre-extracted text folder.

steps.note: The brief carried a PC fact that was half of the answer.
Same as the previous case.
The error text is word for word.
It returns the clinic route. Its text folder does not exist in this repository, and inflate fits some PDFs only.
The subagent window holds it.
The best route needs the PDF entry joined with the Python fact. Sonnet made the join unaided. Opus gave up on the source.
Pages of text appear or they do not.
Sonnet solved it. Opus did not.
Who records the pypdf route, as a sibling or a revision, is not said.
pypdf lives in another app's private runtime, which that app rewrote on 10-21. A stored path to it can change with no event here.

cases.title: Git 'Filename too long' in the scratchpad
cases.story: Refuters cloning repos in the scratchpad hit Windows' 260-character path limit. Six refused alone on 11-03. Next day 15 of 15 clones failed. The tool then shortened the path.
cases.entry: git add, clone or cherry-pick in the scratchpad fails 'Filename too long'. The scratchpad path is about 170 characters. In the throwaway repo run git config core.longpaths true. Check: git add -A succeeds.

steps.note: Refuters were building throwaway repos in the scratchpad. Nothing in their window mentioned it.
A git error in a scratch repo is not a trigger in the earlier knowledge-store design.
'Filename too long' is word for word.
One entry matches exactly.
Siblings run in parallel. A mid-workflow entry reaches only agents started after it, and only by pull.
One flag fixes it.
git add succeeds or it does not.
All agents were Opus.
None of the six had capture duty. Each got out alone. The note came next day from another session after 15 more failures.
A tool update removed the cause about three hours after the note. The note still says the path is about 170 characters.

cases.title: 'Name too long' with a different cause
cases.story: 'ENAMETOOLONG' came from commands over Windows' 32,767-character line limit, not from paths. Two of these contain no git at all.
cases.source: Clinic Opus 11-01; two Sonnet agents 11-04; Codex Sonnet 11-10
cases.entry: The git longpaths entry and the Bash heredoc entry.

steps.note: Agents pasted very large scripts into one Bash call.
Same as before.
The error words name a path. The cause is command length. The query carries the wrong cause.
'name too long' is a piece of 'Filename too long'. The design matches template fragments, so the git entry is the hit.
The match works mechanically.
The git flag cannot shorten a 40k command. A shorter scratchpad path does not either.
The rerun fails again, one wasted call before real diagnosis.
No escalation happens.
The agents' own fix, shorter commands and then Write, was never recorded.
After the path change the git entry is stale for its own symptom, yet still matches this one.

cases.title: A constant-time compare copied to a webhook
cases.story: The ops token gate used hmac.compare_digest on text. Seven days later the same pattern guarded the WhatsApp webhook. A non-ASCII byte turns it into a server error. Review found it 20 days on.
cases.entry: Ops proxy-token gate. A FastAPI dependency reads X-Ops-Proxy-Token. 401 if unset. Constant-time compare with hmac.compare_digest(x or '', expected). 401 on mismatch. Router tests for right, wrong and missing token pass.

steps.note: The later author had the ops gate file in the repository either way.
Nothing failed. Writing new code is not a trigger. The diff warning fires only on stored hazards, and none existed before 07-28.
If asked, 'constant-time compare of a webhook token' is a plain-language query.
It returns the ops gate solution, which contains the defect, stored as solved by a top model.
The match works mechanically.
Copying the stored pattern spreads the defect to a public webhook. That is what happened without a library.
Tests passed. Output equal to the strong model's was the defect.
Both writers were the top rung of their day. The bug surfaced only through a later review.
The 07-28 fix is a clean capture: a safe helper, tests and a CLAUDE.md rule. It can be stored as a do-not-apply entry.
compare_digest also fires on the safe PIN check. Stored tests cover three fixed sites, not a new one.

cases.title: Subagents refused report files
cases.story: A clinic note said subagents cannot write report files. Eleven days later in EMS, eight subagents were refused for report.md. Yet 22 other .md files and 156 .js files were written fine.
cases.entry: Subagents cannot write report files; the harness refuses. Ask them to return the full result in their reply. Earlier Sonnet extractors did write files, so the refusal may depend on agent type or output size.

steps.note: The brief, written by the main session, asks for report.md.
The error fires in the subagent. Its cause is the brief in the main session, which sees no error and has no trigger.
The error text is word for word.
The entry's condition, agent type or output size, is wrong. The record points to the file name.
It is delivered to the one window that cannot change the brief.
Return text. The error message already says so, so the library adds nothing.
The result is immediate.
No escalation happens.
It was captured the same day but too broadly. The writer had two refusals and one counter-example and could not tell which detail mattered.
Read as 'subagents cannot write files', it would push other file writes into replies too.

cases.title: A queued 'ready' could reopen a billed job
cases.story: Job status changes never read the current status. A queued 'ready' replayed after a close reopened a settled, billed job. Tests were green. A technician noticed in production weeks later.
cases.entry: Job lifecycle. Append-only job_event rows. POST /jobs/{id}/transition with action ready, close, abandon, reschedule or haul. Each action updates the job and appends an event. Check: 7 service tests, 4 router tests, 2 real-database tests.

steps.note: A later session got 'wire the bill sheet', which is a task. Nothing in its window says a button can strand a job.
Tests were green. Nothing failed, so nothing asks. The first signal was a technician in production weeks later.
Any query names the task, not the hazard of a 'ready' replayed after 'close'.
'transition' and 'ready' match the old entry, which is the defect. The correct pattern is filed under money words and does not match.
The design does not say whether the entry goes to the session or to a subagent writing one screen.
Adapting the old entry reproduces 'dispatch on the action alone'. Nothing in it says to read the current status.
The old checks test each transition from one state. The every-action-from-every-status matrix came only with the fix. The stored check passes the copy.
No model failed. A technician noticed. The failing parts were written by top models.
Next day a red-team found its freeze parked landed writes as conflicts. Recording before the PR is ready stores the half-right version.
The 07-08 dispatcher handler predates the freeze and never stamps the bill-sent time. A new entry does not look back at existing code.

cases.title: Evidence gate passed with zero bytes
cases.story: A size check swallowed every error and returned 'unknown', so a technician could satisfy the evidence gate without uploading anything. Tests defaulted to 'unknown' and stayed green for 52 days.
cases.entry: Upload size ceiling for pre-signed uploads. At finalize, read the real size with HEAD. Reject anything over the ceiling. A missing object or a temporary error returns None so the caller can fall back to the client's reported size.

steps.note: 'Harden media uploads' is a task. The evidence gate's integrity is not named in it.
The test fixture defaults to 'unknown' and the suite is green. Nothing fails, so nothing looks up.
The task's own words, upload, size and R2, find the entry. Retrieval works and delivers the defect.
Same problem, exact match, wrong answer. The stored text states the mix-up as the design.
The design does not say which window receives the entry.
The cheap model copies 'fall back on None', which the entry calls safe.
The handoff says the no-bytes case was the tested default and nothing asserted existence. The stored check certifies the copy.
No visible failure for 52 days. An adversarial audit found it. Nothing climbs.
The fix rule, None means unknown, never zero, is good. Captured at the first commit, it omits the selfie caller found an hour later.
The handle head_size fires on later diffs to that symbol. The same shape in other words, the mobile bare catch, is a word-level miss.

cases.title: Switching on WhatsApp sending
cases.story: The entry said the dispatcher is safe to switch on. Switching it on would send the whole job history: 36 real messages about months-old jobs. Suppressed rows are permanent.
cases.entry: Customer messages through a transactional outbox. A cursor per consumer drains events in order. The WhatsApp consumer is consent-gated and log-only while settings are empty, so enable_dispatcher stays safe to flip.

steps.note: 'Turn on WhatsApp Cloud sending' is one settings edit, no code. The owner's design speaks of problems a model solves.
Nothing fails before the flip. The flip is the failure. The earlier knowledge-store design has a route for actions. The owner's design names none.
'Enable dispatcher' is the entry's own phrase.
It returns the stored conclusion 'stays safe to flip', at the one moment it can do harm.
The design does not say which window receives the entry.
Acting on it sends the whole history, and suppressed rows are permanent.
No check can say 'safe to flip'. Nothing tested the seed or the age guard. A review found a test that pinned the consent leak.
The author was a top model. Nowhere higher to send it. Later audits found it.
The fix would be stored. But the 08-01 review found three defects inside the fix branch. 'Solved' was the reviewer's call.
After the fix, the action handle is the stated only route to operator hazards. It reaches the next operator.

cases.worked: The correction, once stored, reaches the next operator before an env flip. That avoids a mass-message incident.

cases.title: Login lock that blocks a correct PIN
cases.story: A strong model built a self-healing lock. An audit prescribed a different fix. A third strong model said the audit's fix opens 4-digit PIN guessing. Only an owner decision settled it.
cases.entry: Login lockout. Five failures lock 30 seconds, doubling to a 15-minute cap, always self-healing. A correct PIN during a lock returns 429. Counter survives the error. Per-IP window behind the database lock.

steps.note: 'Fix HANDOFF A2' is a stated problem with file and line. Here the task is a problem.
Applying a fix that a document prescribes is a trigger in the earlier knowledge-store design.
The words line up: lock, correct PIN, 429.
Before the settling commit both hits are wrong. Each came from a strong model and passed its own check.
The design does not say which window receives the entry.
Applying A2 inverts two tests and opens 4-digit PIN brute force. A handful of IPs would finish it in under an hour.
Inverted tests pass. Three strong outputs, two positions. Only an owner decision settled it. 'Equal to the strong model' has no single target.
The wrong fix is silent too. The audit was already a strong-model product. Climbing reaches the tier that wrote it.
The settling commit is a model capture: reason, owner decision and comments on both tests. It can be stored as do-not-apply with owner confirmation.
A document reference on A2 stops the next agent. CLAUDE.md already says so. The clinic's check held the same rule.

cases.title: Opening cutoff rules for cash, pay and stock
cases.story: A rule passed its own tests and an Opus review. Three later root reviews found a double count, a hold that never released, and more. Two correct rules looked like either-or.
cases.source: Cutoff-guards session G10-20; transcript 97380a1e; GC-01, GD-01, GE-03
cases.entry: Opening cutoff guards. One registry of cutoffs, readers per subject. Cash: opening is the balance at the end of the cutoff day. Refuse postings on or before it. Stock: opening is the count when the batch posts. Check: cutoff tests green.

steps.note: G10-20 is a stated gap. Whether stock follows cash on the cutoff day was not known to be a question until GC-01 asked it.
Session tests and its own review passed. Nothing failed until a separate root review, three rounds running.
Good words exist. The deciding detail, an import posted on the count day, is in no query.
It returns a refuted cutoff rule or the half-right stock rule. Two rules, right on different sides, look like either/or.
The finding arrived at 366,229 tokens. The next call read 87,658 after compaction. A fetched entry rides into a summary.
The round-1 fix added a hold. Round 2 found the hold never released. Adapting the rule to new state made a new P1 defect.
Two Opus reviews read the same code and disagreed. The in-session test asserted the double count as correct.
All work was Opus. The working ladder was a root review per round. Nothing failed visibly, so nothing escalated by itself.
Which version is the entry: own review, round 1 or round 2? The first rule's reasoning was compacted before the finding arrived.
The final rule, end of cutoff day for cash, pay and stock, carried unchanged into the real-data switch.

cases.worked: The final rule carried unchanged into the 2026-11-10 real-data switch, reused without re-derivation.

cases.title: Correction form opened blank over a real bill
cases.story: 'Correct the completion' opened a blank form. The server rewrites the bill from the payload, so a blank submit destroyed the bill. A bare catch treated 'offline' and 'no completion' as the same answer.
cases.entry: Completion correction form must not wipe a bill. Load the existing completion and prefill materials, time and remarks. If the fetch fails, return: offline, a blank first completion is still valid. Check: mobile tests green.

steps.note: A stated problem: a blank form wipes a bill.
Tests were green. Nothing fails. The app has no screen-test harness.
A query would say prefill, offline. The governing rule is worded evidence, media counts, None.
The right rule exists and does not match. The same model wrote it 53 minutes earlier in the same PR.
The design does not say which window receives the entry.
The catch says 'offline, a blank first completion is still valid'. A fresh self-written rule did not stop it.
No screen test exists. Logic inside the component is asserted by nothing.
The red-team found it a day later. No model failed.
The fix found three doors, not the one the handoff described, plus a fourth route. An entry written from the audit would be incomplete.
The rule now lives as a tested pure function and in CLAUDE.md. Handles on it fire on later diffs.

cases.title: Advance requests built beside the staff ledger
cases.story: A new advance-request feature reused older ledger patterns. 544 unit tests passed. An Opus audit the next day found stacking races, an actor foreign-key clash and an auto-approve failure.
cases.entry: staff_ledger: append-only staff money. Unsigned amount with a database CHECK. Corrections void and re-log, never edit. Balances only through one repository function. Writes idempotent on a unique client_id. New money columns end in _minor.

steps.note: CLAUDE.md already summarised the earlier tables when 0042 began. The shapes were in the window before any lookup.
Building 0042 raised no error. The design's triggers do not cover request stacking or a system actor.
'Exactly-once disbursement' shares words with the ledger entry. No query asks whether two requests can stack.
Four partial matches come back. The earlier knowledge-store design shows at most one lead and one candidate, so pieces drop out.
The main session pulls the cards into its own window. One session builds the slice.
The working step, a pre-minted client id that becomes the ledger row's id, is in no entry.
544 unit and 7 integration tests passed. The stacking race and auto-approve failure were invisible. An Opus audit added guards next day.
Nothing failed during the task, so nothing was handed up. The fixes came from a later audit outside any ladder.
Stored at 'solved', the entry holds the half-right design. The earlier knowledge-store design's write rule would store nothing. The owner's rule stores the flawed version.
Turning a pay setting on makes the %-of-accrued cap non-binding. The naming rule does not say which style a new key follows.

cases.title: Latest-row-wins ordering by created_at
cases.story: Two writes in one transaction tie on created_at. A real-Postgres CI test caught it in 14 minutes. Four hours later the new rule pointed the next table, 0041, the wrong way.
cases.entry: job_event.seq gives a total order: backfill with row_number, create a sequence, then NOT NULL and UNIQUE. Also: latest-row-wins tables must not order by created_at, because now() ties inside one transaction. Use a monotonic seq.

steps.note: The task, CLAUDE.md and tenancy code held the pattern. The seq pattern lived in 0027's code.
Nothing triggers while designing. In the earlier knowledge-store design, a failure in the shared test run (CI) is a trigger. So a lookup runs only after one CI round.
'Latest row wins per key' shares little with 0027's words. The CI error is a value assertion and names neither now() nor created_at.
0027's entry is the right neighbour but gives no reason against created_at. At 0041 the fresh entry is a wrong match.
The main session is where the design happens.
At 0041 'use a DB sequence' breaks the chain: gaps on rollback, no hash link. 'Never created_at' flags 0041's backfill, which is correct.
The real-Postgres CI test caught the tie in 14 minutes. The check reproduces the cause.
A cheap model facing a wrong-value assertion would escalate. The strong model fixed it in 14 minutes in one commit. Any rung costs more.
The earlier knowledge-store design stores nothing here. The owner's rule stores it, and its general form is too broad for 0041 four hours later.
Within four hours the entry points the next table the wrong way on both its seq and its backfill order.

cases.worked: The real-database test caught the tie in 14 minutes, with a check that reproduced the cause.

cases.title: WhatsApp consumer on an old outbox cursor
cases.story: The new real sender used an old rule: a missing cursor starts at zero and drains all history. Nothing failed while the dispatcher was off. An audit found it 20 days later.
cases.source: Migrations 0027 and 0034; commit da988e2; HANDOFF line 303
cases.entry: Transactional outbox. Each job event carries a running number (job_event.seq), so all events have one order without gaps. The table dispatch_cursor holds one row per consumer. The function run_dispatch_once reads past the last number seen and advances only past accepted events. A scheduler runs it behind enable_dispatcher, default OFF. The WhatsApp consumer is log-only for now.

steps.note: 0034 was built the same day as 0027, both by Fable. The dispatcher code was fresh.
Nothing fails, because the dispatcher is off. No trigger exists for 'a new consumer on an old cursor'.
The builder asked about double-send on replay. The hazard answers a different question: what does the first run do with history?
It returns 0027's entry, the right neighbour, without the start-from-zero warning. That is harmless for a log-only consumer.
The main session window holds it.
The hazard exists only in the merge. It needs an old default, a new real sender, and a permanent first decision per job and kind.
Nothing tested a first run against history. An audit found it 20 days later. The fix landed after 24 days.
No failure was visible, so nothing went up. The finder was a later audit.
The stored conclusion would be 'enable_dispatcher stays safe to flip'. That is wrong, and fetched by anyone about to flip it.
After migration 0046, the earlier knowledge-store design has an action handle. Its diff warnings fired on 13 of 154 past commits.

cases.title: Database locks that were too weak
cases.story: Slice sessions copied an item lock and a 32-bit hash lock. Deadlocks were retried silently. An Opus review and a staging drill found the faults. The kernel later went 64-bit but two copies stayed 32-bit.
cases.when: Built early November 2026; fixes up to 2026-11-06
cases.source: Slice sessions S01, S03, S04, S07; D04-06; F-S02-2
cases.entry: Kernel run_command: one transaction per command. Keys serialized with pg_advisory_xact_lock and hashtext. Retry only on 40001/40P01, at most three times. Open item: hashtext is 32-bit, so a collision serializes unrelated keys. Item lock is select_for_update.

steps.note: Slice sessions open on large context. S07 read 392,125 characters in nine minutes before its lock. S04 averaged about 231k cached tokens per call.
Writing a lock raises no error. The kernel retries deadlocks. select_for_update is too common to pass the selectivity gate.
'Lock the item before posting' finds a lock of the right shape and wrong strength.
The best matches are the defect sources. The sibling is the problem.
The row entered S07's main window nine minutes before the copy, with no compaction between.
S07 wrote the 32-bit lock anyway. The row said 'P3' and named an owner elsewhere. S04 wrote the item lock row FOR UPDATE.
Tests pass, and deadlocks are retried. An Opus review found S04's deadlock by tracing. A staging drill found the hash collision.
The higher tier caught it as a diff reviewer, not because the builder failed and handed up. The builder never knew.
S04 wrote a decision record and a conventions line the same day, naming the sites still wrong. The conventions file did the capture.
S03 merged before S04 learned the rule, and was fixed five days later. The kernel went 64-bit on 11-06. Two copies are still 32-bit.

cases.worked: The slice's own conventions file captured the rule the same day.

cases.title: Mobile offline queues after the jobs outbox
cases.story: The first outbox deleted any write answered with a non-network error. Later queues copied the lesson. The presence queue lacked a 4xx test for three days. Shared code then fixed it.
cases.entry: Mobile outbox v2. A definitive 4xx goes to a visible failed list with Retry or Discard, never auto-deleted. 5xx, 429 and timeouts retry. 401 pauses the queue until re-login. Tag each item with the signed-in tech.

steps.note: The presence task and attendance code were in the window. The outbox lesson lived in the outbox code and the commit body.
Nothing fails. A 403 or 422 leaves a 'pending' badge forever with no error to look up.
The builder's words, 'offline presence outbox', share 'offline' and 'outbox' with the entry.
Presence and punches have the same contract. Pings are similar but not the same, because they are droppable by design.
The main session holds it.
Pings must drop it while 401 still stops the drain. The ping author broke the rule on purpose, not the classification.
Jest tests with a mocked network passed, but none sent a 4xx. The ping gap was found five hours later.
No failure was visible, so nothing went up.
c27bb39 turned the lesson into shared code. CLAUDE.md states the contract and its two droppable exceptions.
Later queues imported the shared check from their first commit and chose park or drop correctly.

cases.worked: Later queues reused the shared classification from their first commit and chose park or drop correctly.

cases.title: Sentry plugin breaks the EAS Android build
cases.story: Adding the Sentry plugin to app.json broke the cloud Gradle build. CI only runs a JavaScript export, so it stayed green. The fix came from comparing with an earlier working build on a side branch.
cases.entry: Trap. EAS Android build errors in 'Run gradlew' after the Sentry package was added to app.json plugins. The plugin adds a Gradle upload step that needs an auth token. Remove it from plugins. The SDK still autolinks. CI cannot see this.

steps.note: Opus 4.8 held the failure and the repo. The decisive fact, that build 14 came from a side branch, was in no window.
'Before retrying a failed build or deploy' fires.
The query is the build log, which reaches a session only when the owner pastes it. The commit quotes only an error code.
An earlier entry comes back as a candidate or as a lead. Nothing exists for the later version bumps.
One card in the calling window, at most 2,000 characters.
Remove one string from app.json plugins. Nothing to adapt.
The real check is the next EAS build, which fails again on three version bumps.
The second failure escalates with only a lookup id. Opus needs a new pasted log and the build-14 comparison. Neither travels in the brief.
The fix meets the write rule, because a build was burned. The version-bump cause is stored as a separate pin.
A phase-close scan labels a stranded fix 'fix not on main'. The auth-token precondition is an EAS-side secret and can never be probed.

cases.title: Empty env value rejected by eas.json
cases.story: A build profile carried an empty Sentry DSN meant as 'off'. EAS rejects empty env values. Every build failed before starting. CI's JavaScript export never reads eas.json.
cases.entry: Trap. Every eas build fails schema validation: an env value is 'not allowed to be empty'. The file eas.json carries EXPO_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN, the crash-report address, as an empty string. Remove the keys; unset already means off. To enable Sentry, add the key with a real DSN.

steps.note: The task was a feature, 'wire the DSN, empty means off', run by Fable. A cheap model shares the blind spot.
At 07-20 the failed build triggers. At 08-03 the diff check runs at the first commit. At 07-18 nothing could fire, because no entry existed.
The EAS message names the key and the rule and is short to paste. At 08-03 the query is the diff itself.
At 07-20 an out-of-vocabulary rule turns a Sentry-word tie into a miss. At 08-03 the entry matches on the eas.json env key.
One warning line and one card in the session's window.
Trivial: the value must be non-empty.
At 07-18 the gate cannot see eas.json validity, and the strong model wrote the defect. A cheap output equal to Fable's is equally broken.
The error explains itself. No escalation is in the record.
This is the design's model entry: the data value is the cause, with a control pair present and absent.
At 08-03 the warning fires and is right. It adds nothing measurable over CLAUDE.md, which already carried the rule.

cases.worked: At 08-03 the diff warning fired at the first commit and was right.

cases.title: Floating base image breaks the Railway build
cases.story: A Dockerfile hardcoded the bookworm package line, but the floating python:3.12-slim image moved to trixie. The image build failed and production stayed on the old version.
cases.source: Commits afb7065, 9c561b0; deploy workflow first run
cases.entry: Trap. Railway image build fails: postgresql-client-17 cannot be installed. The Dockerfile hardcodes the bookworm-pgdg apt line, but python:3.12-slim now follows trixie. Build the line from the image's VERSION_CODENAME. CI does not build this Dockerfile.

steps.note: The first deploy run failed. The writer believed 'bookworm ships 15', the same picture a cheap model brings from training.
'Before retrying a failed deploy' fires.
The apt error sits in the Railway build log. The session may reach the Actions log through gh. The Railway log needs a paste.
First time: the store is empty for this. A miss is the right answer.
Nothing is delivered on a miss.
Nothing to adapt.
The authoritative check is a re-triggered Railway deploy. The strong model's own output was the defect, so 'equal to the strong model' is not success.
Miss, claim, then escalate with the lookup id only. The receiving Opus must fetch the build log again.
It meets the write rule, because a deploy was burned. 'Won't break on the next base-image change' predicts a vendor.
A floating tag moves with no local trace, so the store cannot re-check the entry. The Dockerfile comment carried the lesson at no cost.

cases.title: Staging VM unreachable after a PC reboot
cases.story: After a reboot the Hyper-V switch gets a new address range. The firewall rule allowed ssh only from the old one. The 11-04 entry was half right and spread through three later documents.
cases.source: Staging rig scripts; commit db6c8fa; session S11 lead
cases.entry: Trap (staging rig). After a PC reboot rig.sh start brings the VM up at a new address, then 'ssh did not come up'. The Default Switch gets a new /20 inside 172.16.0.0/12 each boot. The rule must name 172.16.0.0/12.

steps.note: Sonnet 5.5 held the drills task, the rig scripts and the provision script with its comment in a resumed window.
rig.sh start failed after 5 min 23 s, so 'before retrying a failed deploy' fires.
The command output is local. No paste is needed.
It returns the 11-04 entry, which is half right. The error line is a generic ssh wait failure and fits any reason ssh is down.
The card lands in the main window. The compaction summary kept the subnet fact.
The entry's fix was already applied. Nothing to adapt.
The store then learns 'not this entry' for a recurrence of the entry's own cause.
Sonnet solved it in two turns without escalating.
Nothing can test the generalisation from two samples, yet it is stored as fact.
Repair needs two Opus calls for a two-turn Sonnet fix. Cross-project use is not specified. On a real host 'both private blocks' is wrong.

cases.title: Queued writes deleted on a non-network error
cases.story: A fix classified errors by status. Later, Railway's edge answered some requests with 4xx text and phones parked or dropped writes for weeks. No session ran. An agent first saw it on 10-31.
cases.source: Commit c27bb39; O-08-design.md line 62; O-03-design.md line 7
cases.entry: A queued write that synced into a non-network error was deleted. A typed ApiError carries the status. 401 pauses the queue. 400, 403, 404, 409 and 422 are definitive: move to a visible failed list. 5xx, 429 and timeouts retry. Bias every ambiguity toward keeping the record.

steps.note: On 07-03 the task is a real defect in the new queues, and the outbox contract is in the window.
From about 2026-08 phones park and drop for weeks while no session runs. No trigger exists for a failure that never reaches a window.
Nothing to query during the outage. On 10-31 the only text is the host's 'Application not found', which shares no words with any entry.
The diff check surfaces the outbox contract by its identifiers on the changed lines. It is the right entry for the task as posed.
The card sits in the window of the session doing the work.
Adapting to pings, 'droppable, so drop', is what Opus 4.8 did. The output was equal.
Tests mock a 404. Nothing can test who answers a 404. The equal output carried the same exposure.
No visible failure until 10-31. Then the top tier ran the program directly.
The replacement entry comes from a multi-agent workflow. Its premise is dashboard configuration, outside git and outside any footprint.
The vendor change left no local event, so the entry stayed validated. Reuse spread its premise to queues where a 4xx means drop.

cases.title: Old queued completion replays over a newer one
cases.story: An offline completion is replayed over a newer live one. The fix drops the queued copy after a live send. Later it deleted a real queued completion when the live send was a blank form.
cases.entry: Mobile outbox defect. A completion queued offline is replayed over a newer live send under the same stable id. Fix: after a successful live send, remove the queued item. Payments and notes use unique ids, so they never collide.

steps.note: Later tasks are features. The race is not a problem the model has. Only CLAUDE.md's always-loaded known-defect note names it.
No error, so no lookup after failure. The diff check matches named handles on changed lines, and an outbox edit warns.
The diff check is mechanical. The model does not choose the words.
Two entries look like one problem: 'stale write over newer send: fixed' and 'same id, concurrent flush: open'.
One warning line per entry in the main session and the decisions journal. The Opus reviewer rules.
The only stored fix is a rule: on live success, drop the queued copy. Adapting it to a new kind copies the door.
A race's footprint is identical in a good and a bad run. The old Jest case passes even where its rule destroys a bill.
Nothing fails in a session. In the field the winner is whichever request the server finishes last. Nothing climbs. The finder was code reading.
Written at solve time, it is stored with 'never collide' true and the deletion unseen.
The entry stayed true by its own test. A later fix found it was a door through screens outside its footprint.

cases.title: Dispatcher flip sends the whole history
cases.story: Nothing fails until FIXFLOW_ENABLE_DISPATCHER is switched on. Then an unseeded cursor drains 87 events as live WhatsApp messages, 36 of them triggers. Later tasks are a drain audit and a host move.
cases.when: Entry from 2026-08-01 review; ship plan later
cases.source: Commit c731e66; migration 0046; HANDOFF lines 157-166; SHIP-PLAN line 102
cases.entry: Trap, operator action. With no cursor row, run_dispatch_once starts at last_seq=0 and drains all of job_event as live messages. Measured on prod: 87 events, 36 triggers. Fix: migration 0046 seeds the cursor at the latest seq. A 2-day age skip covers a hand reset.

steps.note: Later tasks are a drain audit and a host move. Neither is 'a dispatcher problem'. The hazard is a state the next operator action meets.
No error exists. The diff check cannot see state outside git, such as an env flip or database rows.
The entry's action is 'enable dispatcher'. Later sessions act as drain, restore, re-point or close the window. A hit depends on guessing those verbs.
At best a candidate. Entries about prod data are capped at candidate until a probe and an age-guard test exist.
The main session gets one card.
Events pile up above the July seed while OFF, and months-old writes count as fresh.
The probe runs on a throwaway database migrated to head. It cannot count events above the prod cursor. The 36 came from a prod query.
What must go up is a prod query result, which an operator runs, not a model.
Write-then-approve by a different Opus matched what happened. The review fixed the dead-letter guard, the downgrade and a test that pinned the consent leak.
'Enabling is forward-only' decays with prod rows no footprint item sees. The entry stays validated. The ship plan, not the store, carries the live rule.

cases.title: Clinic check stalls with no test named
cases.story: A parallel check ends 'no test made progress for 600s'. The cause is unknown. The related entry from a faster-check session covers a different cause, a crashed worker. The rerun passed with no fix.
cases.entry: No entry from the 9 Nov stall. The related entry: parallel pass ends 'no test made progress for 600s' after a worker died. Under pytest-xdist loadfile the run hangs. Under load the crash is reported at once. Set DIST_MODE to 'load'.

steps.note: Sonnet was measuring runs mid-task. The log tail, with dots to 96 %, 'exit 1, 961.0s' and the watchdog line, was in the window.
A cheap agent that hits an unexpected gate error looks it up before retrying.
What may matter is not in it. The watchdog reports no test id, and low memory and load show only in load samples.
An exact template hit on the 11-05 entry, a different cause. The ambiguity flag needs more than one recorded cause.
The main session holds it.
Nothing to adapt. The entry only rules out one cause. The model then does what it did without a library: rerun once more.
But the only verdict on the failure is the rerun. It passed with no fix, so 'resolved' is recorded for nothing.
Escalating hands up the same silence: dots, one watchdog line, no test id, no stack, machine state gone. A higher model gets no more evidence.
Nothing is solved, so nothing is written. The next stall starts from zero.
The 11-05 entry stays validated and matches every stall's exact line. Each non-crash stall pays a lookup and a 'not applies'.

cases.title: Flaky clinic tests read random tags as figures
cases.story: Attack tests fail by chance. A number helper reads ids, a CSRF token (a random form value) and random hex tags as money figures. Three writers made three fixes in about 7 hours.
cases.entry: Flaky test, clinic withholding tests. Attack tests S09 and S07 fail by chance when two numbers on a page differ by a hidden amount. The helper numbers() reads ids, the CSRF token and random hex tags as figures. Fix: strip those; a unit test pins what is read and ignored.

steps.note: Sonnet was in a faster-check session. The task is speed. The failing assertion is in the run log.
An unexpected gate error is looked up before retry.
The canonicaliser masks hex runs, ids and free numbers. A figure coinciding with a hex tag is the only clue, and masking removes it.
At 23:49 UTC the test frame hits the root's entry. At 23:00, in a file outside its footprint, a miss is likely.
The main Sonnet session gets a candidate card with a summary and unverified negatives, no fix. The branch lacks the fix commit.
The summary gives the cause, not the fix. The root's fix is half right: a review found its mask 'would hide SYN Till 654321 moved'.
A planted-tag unit test makes the chance repeatable, so a control pair can flip. The session's own check was 'tests passing'.
A second Opus review caught the wrong sequence guess. The same review approved a retry delay that was still over the race window.
Three writers made three fixes for one cause in about 7 hours. The write trigger likely skips the root's routine fix.
In-project, a later test fails at merge naming random_tag, so the entry becomes redundant. Cross-project, FixFlow's backend has no Hypothesis and no uuid4().hex labels.

cases.title: Two pytest runs deadlock on one test database
cases.story: 22 integration tests failed together with no code change. A lone rerun passed. Two pytest processes, from different sessions, shared one test database and deadlocked on its schema setup.
cases.entry: Trap, FixFlow backend tests. Many integration tests fail together (22 in one run) with no code change; a rerun alone passes. Two pytest processes ran against one test database. Never run two pytest processes against that database at once.

steps.note: In FixFlow, a test run with 22 red tests puts the failure in the window.
An unexpected gate error is looked up before retry.
The deciding fact, a second pytest process from another session, is in no log the failing session holds.
At best a candidate. In the clinic, a word match returns a rule with a different mechanism.
In FixFlow the runner can be a subagent in a worktree. Its window starts empty and cannot see the sibling agent holding the lock.
The fix is a rule about other sessions. The failing agent cannot stop the other process. It can only rerun alone.
Process state at the moment of failure is gone once the other process exits. No check, no control pair.
It was traced once. The cost of that trace is recorded nowhere and the session is gone.
HANDOFF traps are seeded as trap entries. A one-line rule is cheap and true in FixFlow.
In the clinic, 'never two at once' contradicts the designed two slots and misses its mechanism, a database drop.

cases.title: Clinic socket refusal retry and its timing
cases.story: A race test failed 2 of 22 runs with 'No buffer space available' on loopback. A 0.05 s retry was added. Reviews found its total delay could make a call look blocked.
cases.when: Commits dd74a3d and 030c6cb; reviews over several hours
cases.source: Commits dd74a3d, 030c6cb; round2.md line 8; task.md lines 105, 344
cases.entry: Gate flake, clinic check on Windows. The serial race pass fails on loopback connect with 'No buffer space available (10055)'. The helper connect_retry retries psycopg.connect up to 6 times, for that message only. Delay is 0.05 s per attempt, under the race window's 0.6 s.

steps.note: A full-check log with a refused connect in a race test is in the window.
An unexpected gate error is looked up before retry.
The error line is exact and distinctive.
Exact template, one recorded cause: a clean hit.
The main session holds it.
Copying the retry copies a hidden coupling: its total delay against another test's timing window. The entry's words and footprint do not name that coupling.
The retry's unit tests pass. The safety claim had no test until later. The race tests it protects passed under load with a broken lock.
An Opus review approved 0.05 s per attempt. The Fable root caught it at the gate. The middle rung endorsed a wrong fix.
Written at solve time, the entry stores the record's false sentence that a retry cannot make a call look blocked.
It was fixed in place within hours. An entry from 030c6cb must be superseded, which needs an Opus actor and a second Opus approver.

cases.title: Carry-in job loop: five faults composing
cases.story: A technician reported a job that never left 'ongoing' and photos re-demanded. Five faults composed into one loop. A cheap fix of the visible fault would have stopped there.
cases.entry: Two technicians can both claim one job. Fix: one atomic conditional UPDATE, unassigned-or-mine and not closed. The loser gets 409 naming the holder. Re-claiming your own job is an idempotent 200 with no second event. Check: two concurrent claims.

steps.note: A field complaint with no error text. Nothing hints that five faults compose.
No error, no failed gate. A cheap model fixes the visible fault and stops. The real signal was the technician hitting it again.
The query is in symptom words. The useful entries are in mechanism words from other slices.
A miss. The design is word-based. The four patterns become relevant only after the loop is split into five faults.
Nothing to deliver. Had all four matched, only one lead and one candidate show.
Had it arrived, the claim guard had to become a transition table and a migration, not a copy. It is also an Opus-reserved area.
594 unit and 131 integration tests were green. A red team found freeze gaps next morning.
The failure signal came from the field, twice. Nothing inside a cheap run would have climbed the ladder.
The captured fix was half right. The later prefill held the next hole. The freeze missed the negotiated-bill field.
The bill-freeze rule it created made the July-08 dispatcher wrong in files the entry never touched.

cases.title: Completion correction wipes a bill; replay conflicts
cases.story: A blank correction form deleted a bill. A replayed completion came back 409 and parked a landed write. A handoff prescribed a guard that closed one route of four.
cases.entry: Correcting a completion wiped the bill, because the server re-prices from the payload. Fix: prefill from the existing completion. Also: a replayed completion came back 409; a byte-identical resubmit is now idempotent. Freeze: bill sent, negotiated, or a payment.

steps.note: The handoff gave file and line and said which guard to reuse.
A fix that a prose register prescribes is a trigger.
The handoff is in the solvers' own words, so word overlap with both entries is high.
The stored fix is the code with the hole, and its old cause reads 'not applies'. The outbox replace-by-id race is in neither.
Two cards fit under 2,000 characters and are pulled into the asking window.
Reading the entry as server protection leaves done-plus-offline open. The first plan's 'last write wins' claim was wrong.
Zero screen tests in 39 suites. The doors live in components nothing asserts.
Nothing fails. A red team caught the wrong plan before coding, not a rung.
The entry is stored with test ids on pure modules. The old entry is superseded, and the stable-id race is an open item.
The refusal depends on the 'unfixed' outbox race existing. Fixing that race in another file changes the entry's meaning. Nothing links them.

cases.title: Dispatcher seams: three items plus a freeze change
cases.story: The July dispatcher entry said safe to flip. Each of three register fixes was right alone. Together they put a resurrected fault inside the error path that fixes it.
cases.source: Commits d1f78cd, 834311f, c731e66, da988e2; handoff items B1-B3
cases.entry: job_event as a transactional outbox with a WhatsApp dispatcher. A cursor drains in seq order. UNIQUE(job_id, kind) guards idempotency. Claim before send. Consent-gated and log-only while settings are empty, so enable_dispatcher stays safe to flip.

steps.note: At the fix there were three register items with file and line and one-line fixes.
The design has a trigger for the fix. A change to the bill-sent time's meaning touched jobs, and the dispatcher was never touched.
The prescriptions share words with the dispatcher entry and the freeze entry.
The top hit is a Fable entry whose safety claims are false. Four parts meet a two-card cap. Nobody says who stamps the bill-sent time.
Pull-only at 2,000 characters means at most two of four parts arrive.
Each fix is right alone. Together one is resurrected inside the error path that fixes it.
A dead-letter test is named for a property it does not exercise. Nothing tests the seed or the age guard.
The error came from the top rung. A second Opus review found the seam. The last question went to the owner and is still open.
The entry was seeded by patch id because its commit is not on main.
The Railway env flip is outside git. The design reaches it only by the 'enable dispatcher' wording. A hand cursor reset has no lookup.

cases.title: Clinic opening cutoff: cash rule vs stock rule
cases.story: A root brief embedded a stock rule that differed from the cash rule. Two partial entries disagreed on what 'cutoff' means. Merging them needed new rules, and no round was solved.
cases.source: Commits 53906e6, c1fb346, b356158; findings GC-01, GE-03; transcript 97380a1e
cases.entry: Cash: opening is the balance at the end of the cutoff day. Refuse postings on or before it, after lock_accounts. Stock: a movement whose event is before a count's observation makes the count stale. Refuse the posting.

steps.note: An 11,840-character brief from the root already embeds the divergent stock rule.
A spec task, no failure. The earlier knowledge-store design's prescription trigger covers prose registers, not a root brief, and that design is FixFlow-only.
If asked, the brief's own words reach both entries.
Two partial entries disagree on what 'cutoff' means. The brief picked the stock one. A review showed the cash rule was right for stock.
Both rules sat in one tool call of the implementing window. Delivery was not the gap.
Holding both, the model kept them apart. The merge needed new rules: no approval on the cutoff day, holds, and set-aside after reversal.
'Root check: 7/7, 1990 passed.' Every stock test posts the day after. A later finding: the book ended right while the period read -10.
Two Opus refute-reviews found it and Fable confirmed. The fix was a choice between two options.
Captured after the first finding, 'stock follows cash and pay' then produced more findings, two of them P1. No round was solved.
The opening's lock order deadlocked with receipts in another module. Cross-project reuse is not specified.

cases.title: Login lock: handoff prescribes the wrong fix
cases.story: A handoff prescribed letting a correct PIN through a lock and inverting two tests. An Opus implementer refused an Opus verifier's fix, and the owner made the final call.
cases.when: Built 2026-07; refused in the settling commit
cases.entry: Five failures lock the account for 30 s, doubling up to 15 min, and the lock heals itself. There is one manager account, so a hard lock would let anyone shut it out. A correct PIN during a lock is refused. A2: public roster plus lock-before-verify lets one wrong PIN per 900 s hold every account. Invert the two pinning tests.

steps.note: The task is a prescription carrying the wrong answer and an instruction to invert two tests.
A trigger fires before applying a register fix.
Prescription wording plus an exact document handle to HANDOFF A2.
First time, both entries point at denial of service. The per-IP window invites the false comfort a later commit refuted.
Two cards, pull-only.
Easy to apply and does damage: a 4-digit PIN with no throttle. A handful of IPs finish in under an hour.
Inverting the two tests as told turns the suite green. Nothing tests the throttle property.
No failure, no climb. An Opus implementer refused an Opus verifier's fix. The owner made the final call.
The entry is do-not-apply with a document reference and protective tests, owner-confirmed. The commit body holds the full argument.
The prohibition is printed, never withheld, while the handoff still prescribes the wrong fix. A new login path would escape the protective test.

cases.worked: A stored do-not-apply entry with owner confirmation prints the prohibition to the next agent.

cases.title: A wrong cause for the three-day halt
cases.story: All clinic sessions stopped on 6 Nov. The top model wrote 'a usage limit stopped every session' unchecked. The real cause was a power-off, shown by a Windows event log. A later lane inherited it.
cases.source: HARNESS-BOTTLENECKS line 397; task.md line 832; card A8-06
cases.entry: All clinic sessions stopped 6 Nov about 14:57; three-day halt. Cause: a usage limit stopped every session. Nothing lost. Recovery: start Docker Desktop, start the nine containers, message each session. Solved by the root, Fable 5.1, 9 Nov.

steps.note: The 11 Nov research lane gets 'find remedies for B03' with the cause in its brief. It has a task, not the problem.
The triggers do not fire for a research lane. The owner's design does not say when research looks up.
The query is built from the brief, so it carries the wrong hypothesis. The right lead, 'unclean shutdown', shares only '6 November'.
The best match is the wrong entry, labelled as solved by the top model. Nothing outranks it.
It is delivered to the lane's subagent window and stays for its short life.
This happened for real through the brief. A lane researched usage-limit pause settings. The later review said the stops were power-offs.
'Equal to the strong model' means equal to a wrong guess. The truth came from data outside git and a brief to attack.
The lane's output looks complete. An Opus 5.5 refuter, a rung below the Fable author, corrected it because of its brief and its data.
Fable wrote the cause 33 seconds after 'Docker down' with nothing checked. Its write rule would exclude the correction too.
Two documents still say 'usage limit'. The evidence is a Windows event log, so nothing watches it for change.

cases.title: Would a graph database cut tokens?
cases.story: A research verdict said no graph database and no cache. The owner said it was not the strongest form. The new question was about joining reasoning branches, a different meaning of 'graph'.
cases.source: Session 0bf1c4f3; HB lines 247-263; HV2 line 371; record #185
cases.entry: Would a graph database with a traversal cache cut tokens in coding sessions? Built a file-level import graph (618 files, 1,119 links). SQLite answers in 0.05 ms. 13 to 14 of 200 searches were connection questions. Verdict: no graph database, no traversal cache.

steps.note: The session held the owner's expectations, his request for graphs where branches can be merged, and the memory index.
No failure triggers a lookup in research. The main session dispatched fact gatherers, a lookup by another name. Neither design says when to do that.
'Graph' in the new question means merging partial solutions during retrieval. In the stored entries it means a code graph for saving tokens.
Five partial matches disagree: withdrawn, narrowed, refuted but unchanged, skipped and unrun. Withdrawn entries are dropped, but one has no link and stays live.
Sonnet gatherers carried the results to the main window. The withdrawal reached it because it sat in the same file as the verdict.
None of the five answers the new question. Verdicts about token saving say nothing about joining reasoning branches.
The standard it failed was to build the strongest form and compare like with like. That standard lived with the owner and in no check.
Only the owner saw the failure, above every rung. The repair cost six research lanes, three verifiers and a critic.
The durable lesson was about method, not graphs, and was stored as a memory note. Negatives need a file footprint. A method lesson has none.
The withdrawal reached one document and memory, not the line saying the PC lacks memory for a graph server. That line was refuted at 07:03Z.

cases.title: Geofence arrival: a ruling, then a blocker
cases.story: A ruling said enqueue the presence row before the location fix resolves. Twenty minutes later a critic with an invariants lens found it loses every crossing's coordinates. The ruling looked final at 21:27.
cases.entry: Problem: the geofence arrival handler overruns its window. Ruling: the phone stops judging; delete the dwell. One bounded fix per crossing. The presence row is enqueued before the fix resolves; the server recomputes every row under R1.

steps.note: The replayed session holds the plan step, which is concrete and names files.
A fix that a prose register prescribes is a trigger.
The query words match the entry's own words.
Suppose the v6 entry was stored and the later fix was not recorded as replacing it. Then the lookup returns v6, marked checked.
The main session receives the entry beside the plan text.
With the v8 entry, applying it is direct. With v6, the implementer enqueues before the fix and every crossing loses its coordinates.
For v6 the gates were written from the same ruling and pass the defect. Only v7 added a failing Jest test.
Two judges and the refuters missed it. A critic at the same tier, with an invariants lens, caught it. The lens decided, not the ladder.
A capture keyed on the commit could store the wrong version: one commit message says v4 and holds v3.
Dependency changes are watched only where the writer names them, and a spike may swap the SDK.

cases.title: The knowledge-store design itself
cases.story: The owner asked for a cache of model reasoning conclusions. The store design was built for exact-repeat defects in one repo. The owner said the review was thinking too narrowly.
cases.source: Design v1.2 and v1.3.1; session 0bf1c4f3; commits 6928828, 140428c; PR #176
cases.entry: Design: a knowledge store for FixFlow agents. A node:sqlite index over an append-only git journal. Declarative probes. Lexical BM25 retrieval, pull-only. A miss is cheap and safe. Embeddings only when the index outgrows a prompt.

steps.note: The session holds the owner's five expectations and a pointer to the design.
The owner's message is the trigger: 'you can find it in the repo hopefully look hard'.
The owner says 'cache library for model reasoning conclusions'. The design calls itself a store of solved defects and traps. Retrieval is word-based only.
The design has versioned entries and supersession, so v1.3.1 comes back, not v1.2.
It arrived as a 132-line Sonnet summary of a 972-line design, a write-up of a write-up.
Built for exact repeats in one repo, it priced the owner's cross-project library. The owner said 'you just deny the possibility'.

cases.title: A lesson ignored hours after it was written

cases.entry: Before judging an idea the owner proposes, research and build its best form and test it fairly. A quick naive prototype against a strong baseline is not a test. Define the scoring first and sweep the parameters.

steps.note: The session held the owner's expectations and the lesson's index line from its first request.

No query. It is pushed.

cases.title: Git clone 'Filename too long' across projects
cases.story: A clinic entry covers long clone paths and a second DLL half. A FixFlow top-model session hit 15 of 15 clone failures. It fixed them inline. The clinic entry is not in the FixFlow store.
cases.entry: Windows: git clone fails 'Filename too long' when the destination root is long. Fix per command: git clone -c core.longpaths=true. Limit: longpaths fixes git only. Native Python modules then fail 'DLL load failed ... filename or extension is too long'. Keep the root under about 100 characters.

steps.note: The main session was on the top tier, not a cheap model. 15 of 15 clone errors were in the persisted output.
A research-script clone is not a trigger in the earlier knowledge-store design. Fable fixed it inline with no rung above. No lookup.
The text 'unable to open loose object: Filename too long' differs from the stored 'cannot create directory'. Only 'Filename too long' overlaps.

One flag. The DLL half is irrelevant to markdown clones and harmless.
Re-running the clone is the real check. No check kind reads a machine path length, so 'applies' is unreachable and the fix text is withheld.
Solved on the first retry.
The DLL half qualifies, but its cause is the clone root, not a commit. FixFlow's writer stored only the git half.
The memory index pushed the fix to siblings. A pull-only lookup would not have fired there. The DLL rule never reached FixFlow.

cases.worked: The memory index pushed the fix to sibling sessions. One later session used the flag on its first clone, with zero failures.

No climb. The refusals were absorbed as returned text.

A hedge, a flat rule, a paste to FixFlow, then 'They can', then 8 refusals next day. Nothing links refusals to the refutation.

steps.note: The FixFlow rule was in the window at line 3. The actor is the top-tier orchestrator.

It was already in the main window.
The rule was present and not carried to the neighbouring tool, three times.

The actor is the top rung and the failure is overspend. The ladder climbs on failure and does not see it.

cases.entry: Clinic full check on Windows is latency-bound, not CPU-bound. Pytest in a Linux container beside Postgres: 230.1 s vs 367.2 s native. Owner decision USER-23: tests go to a Linux container next to the database. Measure before serialising.

cases.title: Race tests that pass without their lock
cases.story: Race tests named a lock but passed with that lock removed, because a counter row serialized the work. The lesson was in every brief and followed in form. Nine of 11 gates took three rounds.
cases.when: Clinic gates G02-02 to G10-23, early November 2026
cases.source: Clinic slice S04 session a9b52f2e; check-summary.md line 75; task.md line 303
cases.entry: A race test names a lock but passes with that lock removed. Both postings call open_document, which updates a per-type counter before any lock, so the counter serializes them. Rule: a race test proves a lock only if it fails with that lock removed. Method: remove one lock at a time.

steps.note: The slice held the root's brief, which said to record a lock-removal experiment per race. The task is tests to write, not a problem.
Nothing fails. A cheap model gets no signal and the ladder never starts. The root pushed the lesson into briefs outside the fetch path.
Task words reach the S02 entry. For S08 the words share only 'race' and 'lock' with it.
Later failures share the claim, not the cause. Their causes differ: a counter row, a helper after deferred checks, a trigger lock. Others were an earlier variant and no single lock.
The design does not say which window gets the entry. The error was made by read-only Opus reviewers and the Fable root.
The lesson was in every brief and followed in form. They held after deferred checks, ran on an earlier variant, or removed the wrong layer.
What decided was a reviewer reading, then model-run experiments, at least four later shown misleading.
Opus reviewers noticed and handed up finding tables. The Fable root's round-1 premise was wrong. Removing locks one at a time settled it.
Round 1 said scope lock, round 2 counter, round 3 proved counter. A capture at the strong model's verdict stores the wrong lock.
Any added guard changes the answer without touching the test. Race footprints are identical in good and bad runs.

cases.title: A reversal test leaves the database short

A query in those words finds the real-data guard, not a migration test in another file.
The nearest stored items are the earlier test, a latent defect, and a rows-left-behind fix. That fix does not cover schema state.
The failure arrived in the Fable root's main window as test output and stayed through the fix.
Reuse multiplied the defect. The session copied the template's finally into two new tests.
2570 passed on the branch; 2 of 2570 failed on the merged tree. The check that judges equality certified a wrong solution.
A red deterministic check, not a model, noticed it. The handoff was tool output. Fable fixed it in about a minute.
The root wrote the rule into conventions within two minutes. Under the design's write rule, this one-attempt top-tier fix is routine and not recorded.
The entry covers one reversal helper. A reversal written another way, or failing on another constraint, shares no words. The 12-worker prediction is untested.

cases.title: Subagent writes: the probe overruled two Opus

cases.entry: Subagents launched with the Agent tool could not write their reports. Both Opus analysts said the harness blocks subagents from writing report files and returned the text. Sonnet extractors wrote files earlier, so it may depend on agent type or output size. Brief subagents to return the result.

The task was the question itself, so a lookup had a clear trigger.
'Subagent write file refused' matches the entry's words.
The entry carried a paraphrase, not the tool error, and its hedge pointed at the wrong variables.
The entry sat in the root's main window and stayed there through the compile.
It called the rule an unchecked self-report. The probe tested another condition.
The refusal text that decides it sat in 1 Nov transcripts, never read.
The ladder ran downward. A Haiku probe overruled two Opus observations and the Fable root sided with the probe. The original observers were right.
Each write widened or flipped the entry: 'report files', then 'file writes are refused', then 'They can'. Two contradictory entries, neither naming the condition.
They adapted silently and the root never saw it. The saved compile keeps 'They can' and a remedy the refusal blocks.

cases.title: A 'not found' that was a search gap
cases.story: A critic searched task.md files, found no 34-minute wait, and called the owner's figure unsupported. The wait was printed in a root transcript never searched. A wider refuter corrected it.

The lanes did not decide to look anything up. The design does not say whether a negative is pushed or fetched.
'34 minutes' and 'slot wait' hit the critic's entry exactly.
Exact match, wrong answer. The entry is a 'not found' whose scope excluded the root transcript where the check printed 'waited 2030 s'.
One entry reached four parallel map lanes and the verdict writers at once, before anything checked it.
'Not in task.md' became 'in no file', then 'the owner's figure is wrong', then a stop rule.

Caught by a same-tier Opus-high refuter with a refute-by-default brief and a wider search, not by a higher tier.
One verdicts file still says 742 s. The 9 Nov observation was a measurement, not a solved problem, so no capture rule would store it.
The 742 s copy survives in the evidence file a trial would run from.

cases.title: Sentry plugin trap, first moment
cases.story: Build 15 failed in Gradle after the Sentry plugin was added. Two causes shared one symptom. The fix commit never reached main. The real session found both causes in one pass.
cases.entry: EAS Android build errors in 'Run gradlew'. Cause: expo install added the Sentry config plugin to app.json. That wired in a Gradle step needing an auth token, org and project. Fix: drop the plugin. Holds while no Sentry project or token exists. CI cannot see this.

'Before retrying a failed build' is a named trigger.
The generic error code is flagged ambiguous. Without the pasted Sentry line, the query reaches a candidate at most.
Two causes, one symptom. One entry matches the stranded plugin. The Dependabot SDK pins have no entry, and nothing says a second cause exists.
Pulled into the main session that owns the build. On a miss only the lookup id goes into the brief.

After removal the plugin probe reads absent while the build still fails on the Dependabot pins. The only full check is another EAS build.
A second failing build is visible, and the miss on the second cause escalates as it does today.
The commit says the plugin re-entered main via #59, but the fix commit never reached main. The fix-reached-main check catches the anchor, not the prose.
A phase close would print 'fix not on main' as one of four counts. The design does not say who must act on that line.

cases.title: Sentry trap: copied rule loses its condition
cases.story: The June note said re-add the plugin once a Sentry project and token exist. A July writer copied it into CLAUDE.md as 'must never be added'. August wired a real DSN without the plugin.
cases.entry: The first Sentry entry, plus the 06-26 text: re-add the plugin only once a Sentry project and auth token exist. Dependabot was told to ignore the Expo and RN native family.

steps.note: Task windows have CLAUDE.md always loaded. On 08-03 it holds both traps and the PR cites them.

On 08-03 the changed line, the env key in eas.json, is a usable diff query.
07-18: a miss, because it is the first time. 08-03: a correct but idle warning. Nothing surfaces the plugin entry's now-relevant condition.
Warning lines go to the PR's decisions journal and to the Opus reviewer.
On 08-03 the agent had already obeyed CLAUDE.md. The store adds a warning, a verify run and a reviewer ruling, and saves nothing.
The empty-value entry is a probe on parsed eas.json, and 'absent' is right. A test capture to the real project proved the DSN.
Nothing failed on 08-03.
The 07-18 writer copied the condition into the always-loaded file as 'must never be added'. The store's entry keeps the precondition. Two versions exist.
The Sentry project was created outside git, so no event fires. If asked, the entry says inconclusive both before and after. CLAUDE.md still says never.

cases.worked: On 08-03 the diff warning fired and was right, though the agent had already obeyed CLAUDE.md, so it saved nothing.

cases.title: A false 'each job is idempotent' sentence
cases.story: A truth pass wrote that every scheduler job is idempotent. It was false when written: the orphan sweep mints a fresh client id each run. An audit found it 20 days later. It still stands.
cases.source: Commits 85c88c0, 8ce9530, da988e2; HANDOFF A7; CLAUDE.md line 312
cases.entry: Scheduler jobs: weekly payroll export, nightly backup, daily auto-link scan and daily media-orphan sweep. Also a 300 s metric rollup, and the dispatcher (default OFF). Each is idempotent, so a duplicate run is harmless.

steps.note: On 08-02 both documents were in the window: CLAUDE.md always, and the HANDOFF because the PR edits it.
The diff check joins code and config files only, so no lookup happens.
No lookup happens, so no query exists.
If one had run, the store would miss. The register item is unsolved, and entries are written only when solved.
No lookup happens, so nothing is delivered.
The correction was in the window as prose and did not reach the edit.
The line stood 20 days, until an audit whose default verdict was REFUTED found it. That audit is the expensive-model judge.
No failure is ever raised. The sweep re-alarms silently, and nothing reads the alarms.
The strong model's summary was written from reading, not checked, 86 minutes after the contradicting code landed.
The refuted line was rewritten five days after the refutation and still stands on 11-12. Contradictions are corrected only at seeding.

cases.title: Stored 'no Python' read as a hypothesis
cases.story: The memory index says no python on PATH. Later subagents treated it as a hypothesis and probed with a fallback in one command. The error line appeared, but the library had worked.
cases.entry: One note: a Python 3 exists in the Codex runtime folder; the earlier 'no Python' note was wrong. Another: python is not on PATH in Git Bash (Store alias); use node for JSON. The index line ends 'no python on PATH'.

'Python was not found' is an exact, stable string.

The fallback's output came back in the same tool result.

The 11-04 note said 'not on PATH' three days after the 11-01 note called an earlier 'no Python' wrong. Neither knew uv arrived 11-02.
python is still a Store stub. uv is on PATH, and newer Pythons appeared later. No note changed, and no event exists for machine changes.

No escalation in the record.

cases.title: Clinic memory says 'no uv'; uv arrives that night
cases.story: A probe recorded no uv and no Python 3.13. uv and 3.13 were installed that same evening. Three projects wrote three scoped notes. 86 windows started within 22 minutes.

cases.entry: Machine facts probed 2026-11-02: no Python 3.13, no uv, no pipx, no py launcher. The only Python is the Codex runtime 3.12.14 at its folder path. The EMS note of 11-01 had the same path.

Three projects, three writers, three scopes. They wrote 'no uv' before uv arrived, 'not on PATH, use node', and 'no Python on the machine'. The last was false when written.
